danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 32
paragraphs: Ude af sig selv af rædsel sprang Pierre op og løb tilbage til batteriet som det eneste tilflugtssted fra de rædsler, der omgav ham.

Da han trådte ind i forskansningen, bemærkede han, at der var folk, der foretog sig noget, men at der ikke blev fyret fra batteriet. Han nåede ikke at forstå, hvem disse mænd var. Han så den ældre officer ligge på jordvolden med ryggen til, som om han undersøgte noget nedenfor, og han så, at en af de soldater, han tidligere havde lagt mærke til, var sluppet fri af dem, der holdt ham, og skreg »Brødre!« — og han så noget andet mærkeligt.

Han nåede imidlertid ikke at forstå, at obersten var blevet dræbt, at soldaten, der råbte »Brødre!«, var taget til fange, og at en anden lige for øjnene af ham var blevet stukket i ryggen med en bajonet. For knap var han løbet ind i skansen, før en mager, gusten mand i blå uniform kom farende imod ham, badet i sved, med sablen i hånden og råbende et eller andet. De havde begge løbet i fuld fart mod hinanden, før de fik øje på hinanden, og for at tage af for stødet strakte Pierre uvilkårligt hænderne frem og greb manden, en fransk officer, om skulderen med den ene hånd og om struben med den anden. Officeren tabte sin sabel og greb Pierre i kraven.

I nogle sekunder stirrede de med skræmte øjne på hinandens fremmede ansigter, og begge var forvirrede over, hvad de havde gjort, og hvad de skulle gøre. »Er jeg taget til fange, eller har jeg taget ham til fange?« tænkte de begge. Men franskmanden var tydeligvis mere tilbøjelig til at tro, at det var ham, der var fanget, for Pierres stærke hånd, drevet af ufrivillig frygt, greb stadig fastere om hans hals. Franskmanden ville sige noget, men i samme øjeblik fløj en kanonkugle med et uhyggeligt lavt hvæs henover dem, og det var, som om den rev hovedet af franskmanden — så hurtigt dukkede han sig.

Pierre bøjede ligeledes hovedet og slap sine hænder. Uden at tænke mere over, hvem der havde taget hvem til fange, løb franskmanden tilbage til batteriet, og Pierre løb ned ad skråningen og snublede over døde og sårede, der syntes at gribe fat i hans fødder. Men før han nåede bunden af bakken, kom tætte rækker af russiske soldater ham i møde; de løb i uorden, faldt, snublede, råbte og galoperede muntert og stormende op mod batteriet. (Det var det angreb, Jermolóv (general Jermolóv) senere tog æren for ved at hævde, at kun hans mod og held havde gjort det muligt, idet han påstod, at han havde kastet de Sankt Georg-kors, han bar i lommen, op på bakketoppen og beordret tropperne til at tage dem.)
De franske, der havde besat batteriet, flygtede, og vore tropper forfulgte dem under råbet »Hurra!« — så langt hinsides batteriet, at det var svært at kalde dem tilbage.

Fangerne blev ført ned fra batteriet, og blandt dem var en såret fransk general, som officererne samlede sig om. Skarer af sårede — nogle Pierre kendte, andre ikke — russere og franskmænd med fortrukne ansigter af smerte, gik, kravlede og blev båret på bårer fra batteriet. Pierre gik op til bakketoppen, hvor han havde tilbragt over en time, og af den familiekreds, der havde taget imod ham, fandt han ingen. Der var mange døde, som han ikke genkendte. Men nogle genkendte han. Den unge officer sad stadig sammenfaldet ved kanten af jordvolden i en pøl af blod. Den rødmussede soldat rørte sig endnu, men de bar ham ikke bort.
Pierre løb ned ad skråningen endnu en gang.
»Nu holder de op med det, nu vil de blive forfærdede over, hvad de har gjort!« tænkte han og gik formålsløst hen mod en flok bæremænd, der bevægede sig bort fra slagmarken.

Men bag røgens slør stod solen stadig højt, og foran og især til venstre, nær Semjonovsk, syntes noget at syde i røgen, og tordenen af kanoner og musketild aftog ikke, men voksede endda til en desperat styrke som en mand, der med al sin kraft skriger ud i vild anstrengelse.

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 32
paragraphs: Beside himself with terror, Pierre jumped up and ran back to the battery as the only refuge from the horrors surrounding him.

Entering the earthwork, he noticed men doing something there but no shots being fired from the battery. He didn't have time to register who these men were. He saw the senior officer lying on the earth wall with his back turned, as if examining something below, and that one of the soldiers he'd noticed before was struggling forward shouting "Brothers!" while trying to free himself from men holding his arm. He saw something else strange too.

But he didn't have time to realize that the colonel had been killed, that the soldier shouting "Brothers!" was a prisoner, or that another man had been bayoneted in the back before his eyes — because hardly had he run into the redoubt when a thin, sallow-faced, sweating man in a blue uniform rushed at him sword in hand, shouting something. Instinctively bracing against the impact — for they had been running at full speed toward each other before either saw the other — Pierre put out his hands and seized the man (a French officer) by the shoulder with one hand and by the throat with the other. The officer dropped his sword and grabbed Pierre by the collar.

For several seconds they stared with frightened eyes at each other's unfamiliar faces, both bewildered by what they had done and what to do next. "Am I the prisoner, or have I taken him prisoner?" each was thinking. But the French officer was more inclined to think he'd been captured, because Pierre's strong hand, driven by instinctive fear, squeezed his throat ever tighter. The Frenchman was about to say something when, just above their heads, a cannonball whistled by — terribly low — and it seemed to Pierre that the French officer's head had been torn off, so fast had he ducked.

Pierre ducked his head too and let his hands fall. Without further thought about who had captured whom, the Frenchman ran back to the battery and Pierre ran down the slope, stumbling over the dead and wounded who seemed to clutch at his feet. But before he reached the bottom of the knoll, he was met by a dense crowd of Russian soldiers who, stumbling, tripping, and shouting, ran merrily and wildly toward the battery. (This was the attack for which Ermolov claimed credit, declaring that only his courage and luck made such a feat possible — the attack during which he supposedly tossed St. George's Crosses from his pocket into the battery for the first soldiers who reached it.)
The French who had occupied the battery fled, and our troops, shouting "Hurrah!" chased them so far beyond the battery that it was hard to call them back.

The prisoners were brought down from the battery, including a wounded French general whom the officers surrounded. Crowds of wounded — some Pierre knew, some he didn't — Russians and French alike, with faces twisted in pain, walked, crawled, and were carried on stretchers from the battery. Pierre went back up onto the knoll where he had spent over an hour, and of that family circle that had welcomed him as a member, not a single one remained. There were many dead he didn't recognize, but some he knew. The young officer still sat the same way, doubled over, in a pool of blood at the edge of the earth wall. The red-faced man was still twitching, but they didn't carry him away.
Pierre ran down the slope once more.
"Now they will stop it — now they will be horrified at what they have done!" he thought, walking aimlessly toward a crowd of stretcher-bearers moving from the battlefield.

But behind the veil of smoke the sun was still high, and in front — especially to the left near Semenovsk — something seemed to be seething in the haze, and the roar of cannon and musketry did not weaken but grew even more desperate, like a man straining to scream with all his remaining strength.
